=== cap-http-01 | The simulated network: streams, latency and chunking
--- teach
In Computer Networks you built a small HTTP server over an in-memory network: generator tasks took turns in a round-robin scheduler, and `yield` meant "I cannot go on yet". This capstone builds the real thing. Over thirteen milestones you will write an HTTP/1.1 server for ORBIT's ground station, with a parser that survives any input, routing, keep-alive, static files, a JSON API, timeouts and graceful shutdown. Then you will prove it under load with a load tester of your own, and protect it with a rate limiter. The finished project is over 2,000 lines, and every milestone's tests must pass before the next one starts.

This first milestone builds the ground everything stands on: a simulated network that behaves like TCP.

### The plan

| milestone | what you build |
|---|---|
| 1 | the simulated network: streams, latency, chunking |
| 2, 3 | an incremental request parser: the head, then bodies |
| 4 | responses, and a parser for them on the client side |
| 5, 6 | the server and a client; keep-alive, pipelining, real sockets |
| 7, 8 | a router, then middleware |
| 9, 10 | static files with Range requests, then a JSON API |
| 11 | timeouts, connection limits and graceful shutdown |
| 12, 13 | a load tester with latency percentiles, then a rate limiter |

Each milestone's starter is the whole project so far, exactly as the last milestone's solution left it, plus empty stubs for the new parts. So a bug you left behind never follows you: you always start from a working project.

### Why simulate the network?

ORBIT runs Python in the browser, where there are no sockets. But even with sockets, a good engineer would simulate here, for three reasons.

- **Adversarial input on demand.** Real TCP on one computer usually delivers a whole request in one piece, so the bug "I assumed one read is one request" hides until production. The simulation can hand over every request one byte at a time.
- **Time you control.** A test of "the server gives up on a client after 30 seconds" should not take 30 seconds. Here it takes a millisecond.
- **The same result every run.** A test that fails only sometimes is worse than none. Nothing here depends on the real clock or on the operating system's timing.

Serious systems are tested this way: see [[deterministic simulation testing|dst]].

### From generators to asyncio

In the networks course, a task that had to wait ran `yield`, and your `run` function gave the next task a turn. Python's **asyncio** is the same idea, grown up: a **coroutine** is a function defined with `async def`, and `await` marks the places where it may pause. The **event loop** plays the part of your scheduler.

| Computer Networks, lesson 13 | this capstone |
|---|---|
| `recv` raises `BlockingIOError`, the task runs `yield` and tries again later | `data = await stream.read()` pauses until data has arrived |
| `run(*tasks)`, round robin | the asyncio event loop |
| a task yields a generator to start it | `asyncio.create_task(coroutine)` |
| `StreamNetwork(chunk)` | `Network(latency, chunk)` |

The big difference is that nothing spins. Your old tasks retried `recv` on every turn, even when nothing had arrived. A coroutine that awaits is not run at all until something wakes it.

### Simulated time

A normal event loop, when every task is waiting, asks the operating system to sleep until the next timer is due, through a call named [[select|select]]. The starter's `SimLoop` (given, in Part 1) replaces that one step: instead of sleeping, it moves its clock forward to the next timer. So `await asyncio.sleep(30)` takes no real time, and `now()` reads the simulated clock.

```python fragment
async def two_waits():
    await asyncio.sleep(1.5)
    first = now()
    await asyncio.sleep(0.25)
    return first, now()

run_sim(two_waits())        # (1.5, 1.75), instantly
```

`run_sim(coroutine)` is the simulated `asyncio.run`: it makes a fresh loop with the clock at 0, runs the coroutine to the end, cancels anything left over, and returns the result. If every task is waiting and no timer is set, nothing can ever happen again, so it raises `RuntimeError("deadlock ...")` instead of hanging. That makes a whole class of bugs show up as a clear error.

### The interface: a stream

A connection has two ends. Each end is a **stream** with these operations:

- `await read(n)`: up to `n` bytes that have arrived, waiting if none have. It returns `b""` at **EOF**, when the other end will send nothing more.
- `write(data)`: send bytes. It does not wait.
- `await drain()`: wait until it is sensible to write more. Here it returns at once.
- `write_eof()`: send EOF but keep reading, a [[half-close|half-close]].
- `close()`: send EOF, stop reading, and drop anything unread.

This is exactly the shape of asyncio's own `StreamReader` and `StreamWriter` for real sockets. That is deliberate. In milestone 6 a ten-line adapter will run the same server on real sockets, which is the whole point of simulating behind an interface instead of inside the server.

### How bytes travel

**Latency** is the time data takes to reach the other end. A write must not appear at the other end at once; it must land `latency` seconds later. So each end keeps two things:

- `_buffer`, a `bytearray` of bytes that have **landed** and are waiting to be read;
- `_in_flight`, a `deque` of items **travelling** towards it: `bytes`, or `None` for EOF.

Writing on one end calls `_travel(item)` on the other end. That appends the item to `_in_flight` and sets a timer with `loop.call_later(latency, self._land)`. When the timer fires, `_land` moves the **oldest** item in flight into the buffer (or notes EOF) and wakes a reader.

Why does `_land` take the oldest item, instead of each timer carrying its own piece of data? Because timers that are due at the same moment [[may fire in any order|timer-ties]]. Two writes in the same instant get timers with the same deadline, and if each timer carried its own data, `b"GET"` then `b" /"` could land as `b" /GET"`. With the queue, the timers only say "one more item is due"; the order comes from the deque.

**Why the stream is correct.** The invariant: *the bytes read so far, then the buffer, then the bytes in flight, in that order, are exactly the bytes written so far, in the order they were written.*

- At the start, nothing has been written and all three are empty.
- A write appends to the end of the in-flight queue, the end of the order. The invariant holds.
- A timer moves the front item of the queue to the end of the buffer. The order does not change.
- A read removes bytes from the front of the buffer and adds them to what has been read. The order does not change.

So a reader receives exactly what was written, in order, however the timers fire and however the reads cut it up. EOF travels in the same queue, so it can never overtake data.

### Waiting and waking

A reader with nothing to read must pause until `_land` adds something. The tool is an asyncio **[[future|future]]**: a box that will hold a result later. The reader creates one, stores it in `self._waiter`, and awaits it. `_land` calls `self._wake()`, which puts a result in the box, and the event loop resumes the reader, which checks the buffer again. The small class `_Waitable` holds this: `_wait()` and `_wake()`. Only one task may wait at a time; a second one raises `RuntimeError`, because two tasks reading one connection would each get random pieces of the other's data.

Two alternatives were rejected. Polling (`while not self._buffer: await asyncio.sleep(0.001)`) wastes work, and in simulated time it moves the clock in tiny steps for no reason. An `asyncio.Event` would work, but needs care to clear it at the right moment; a fresh future for each wait cannot be left set by accident.

### Chunking

`read(n)` returns at most `min(n, chunk, bytes in the buffer)` bytes. With `Network(chunk=1)`, every read returns one byte, which is how later milestones will prove that your parser does not assume anything about how a request is cut up.

### Connecting, listening and closing

- `net.listen(addr)` makes a **listener** at an address, a pair like `("orbit.local", 80)`. A second listener at the same address raises `OSError`, as a real `bind` does.
- `await net.connect(addr)` costs one round trip, like TCP's handshake: `latency` for the request to arrive, then `latency` for the answer to come back. If nobody listens there when the request arrives, it raises `ConnectionRefusedError` after that round trip. Otherwise the listener gets the server's end in its queue of pending connections, and the client gets its own end.
- `await listener.accept()` returns the oldest pending connection, waiting for one if there is none.
- `listener.close()` stops listening: new connections are refused, connections still pending are closed (their clients see EOF), and a task waiting in `accept` gets `OSError`.
- On a stream, `close()` sends EOF to the other end. Data that lands on a closed stream is dropped, as a real socket drops data for a closed connection.

### What it costs

- `write` is O(1) plus copying the data, O(n) for n bytes: one append and one timer.
- A timer costs O(log t) with t timers waiting, because the event loop keeps them in a heap.
- `read` of k bytes is O(k): a slice, and a delete from the front of the `bytearray`, which CPython does without moving the rest.
- Memory is the bytes in flight and in buffers. A real network limits both, which is what `drain` is for on a real socket; here they are unlimited, and milestone 11 is where the server protects itself.

### How the checks test it

The starter's **test tools** (given, at the end of the file) drive the network, and the checks call them:

- `together(a, b)` runs two coroutines at the same time and returns both results.
- `script(net, addr, steps)` is a scripted client: steps like `("send", b"GET")`, `("wait", 0.5)` and `("eof",)`. It returns everything it received and the time the other side closed.
- `recorder(listener)` accepts one connection and returns every piece it read, with the time it arrived. `echo(listener)` sends back whatever it receives.
- `sequence(...)` runs small steps in order, and turns an exception into its name, so a check can say "this read raises `OSError`".

**Watch out:** the classic bugs in a simulated (or real) network layer.

- Letting each timer carry its own data. It passes every test with one write, and scrambles bytes as soon as two writes happen in the same instant.
- Forgetting to wake the reader after data lands, or after `close()`. The reader then waits forever, which `run_sim` reports as a deadlock.
- Treating EOF as an error. `b""` is the normal end of a stream, and every later read returns `b""` again.
- Returning more than `chunk` bytes from one read. The tests in later milestones depend on tiny pieces being really tiny.

::: context dst Deterministic simulation testing
FoundationDB, a distributed database now owned by Apple, was built by first writing a simulator of its whole cluster: networks, disks and clocks, all fake and all driven by one random seed. Engineers ran millions of simulated days, with packets lost and machines crashing on purpose, and any failure could be replayed exactly from its seed. TigerBeetle and other modern databases work the same way. Your network is a small version of the idea: every run of a check sees exactly the same bytes at exactly the same simulated times.
:::

::: context select What the event loop waits in
A real event loop keeps a list of sockets and timers. When no task can run, it calls the operating system through `select`, `epoll` on Linux or `kqueue` on macOS, with a timeout: "wake me when any of these sockets has data, or after this many seconds, whichever comes first". Everything else in asyncio is bookkeeping around that one call. `SimLoop` overrides only that step, so the rest of asyncio, including `sleep`, `wait_for` and `gather`, works unchanged on simulated time.
:::

::: context half-close Sending EOF but still listening
TCP has two directions, and each can be closed on its own. A client can say "I have sent everything" with `shutdown(SHUT_WR)`, which sends a FIN, and still read the server's answer. Some old protocols relied on this: the client sent a request, half-closed, and the server read until EOF. HTTP/1.1 frames its messages with lengths instead, so it rarely needs half-closes, but a robust server must still cope with a client that half-closes after its last request.
:::

::: context timer-ties Why timers due together can come out in any order
The event loop keeps its timers in a heap, the structure from DSA I, ordered by the time each is due. A heap is not stable: when several items have the same key, popping them one by one returns them in no particular order. Scheduling ten timers for the same moment in CPython fires them as 0, 2, 6, 5, 9, 8, 7, 1, 3, 4. Anything that depends on the order of equal timers is a bug waiting for a busy moment.
:::

::: context future Futures: a box for a later result
An asyncio future is an object that starts empty and is filled once, with a result or an exception. A coroutine that awaits an empty future pauses; when some other code calls `set_result`, the event loop schedules the coroutine to continue, and `await` gives back the result. Tasks, `sleep` and the streams of real sockets are all built from futures. Calling `set_result` on a future that is already filled raises an error, which is why `_wake` first checks `done()`.
:::
--- task
Build Part 2 of the starter: the simulated network. The starter's Part 1 (`SimLoop`, `run_sim`, `now`) and the test tools at the end are given; keep them as they are.

**`_Waitable`**, a base class with a class attribute `_waiter = None`:
- `async _wait()`: raise `RuntimeError` if another task is already waiting; otherwise store a new future (`asyncio.get_running_loop().create_future()`) in `self._waiter`, await it, and set `self._waiter` back to `None` when done, even if the wait was cancelled.
- `_wake()`: if a task is waiting and its future is not done, give the future a result (`None`).

**`Network(latency=0.0, chunk=65536)`**: raise `ValueError` if `latency < 0` or `chunk < 1`. Keep `latency`, `chunk` and a dict `listeners` from address to listener. Client ports start at 50000 and go up by one for each connection.
- `listen(addr)`: `addr` is turned into a tuple. `OSError` if something already listens there; otherwise make a `Listener`, remember it and return it.
- `async connect(addr, host="client")`: sleep `latency`. If nobody listens at `addr` now, sleep `latency` again and raise `ConnectionRefusedError`. Otherwise make two `Stream`s: the client's, with local address `(host, port)` and remote address `addr`, and the server's, the other way round. Make each the other's `peer`, hand the server's stream to the listener with `listener._arrive(stream)`, sleep `latency` again, and return the client's stream.

**`Listener(net, addr)`**, a `_Waitable`, with `net`, `addr`, `closed = False` and a deque of pending streams:
- `_arrive(stream)`: add it to the pending ones and wake a waiting `accept`.
- `async accept()`: return the oldest pending stream, waiting while there is none. Raise `OSError` when there is none and the listener is closed.
- `close()`: do nothing if already closed. Otherwise mark it closed, remove it from `net.listeners`, close every pending stream, and wake a waiting `accept`.

**`Stream(net, local, remote)`**, a `_Waitable`, with `net`, `local`, `remote`, `peer = None`, `closed = False`, a `bytearray` buffer, a deque of items in flight, and flags for EOF received and "can still send":
- `write(data)`: `OSError` if the stream is closed or has sent EOF. Otherwise, if `data` is not empty, call `self.peer._travel(bytes(data))`.
- `async drain()`: `OSError` if closed; otherwise return.
- `write_eof()`: the first time only, stop sending and call `self.peer._travel(None)`.
- `async read(n=65536)`: `ValueError` if `n < 1`. While the buffer is empty and no EOF has landed, raise `OSError` if the stream is closed, else wait. Then raise `OSError` if the stream is closed. Return and remove the first `min(n, net.chunk, len(buffer))` bytes, which is `b""` at EOF.
- `close()`: do nothing if already closed. Otherwise send EOF (as `write_eof` does), mark it closed, empty the buffer, and wake a waiting reader.
- `_travel(item)` (called on the receiving end): append `item` to the items in flight, and call `self._land` after `net.latency` seconds with `asyncio.get_running_loop().call_later`.
- `_land()`: take the **oldest** item in flight. If the stream is closed, drop it. Otherwise `None` means EOF has landed, and bytes are added to the buffer; then wake a waiting reader.
--- starter
"""ORBIT ground station: an HTTP/1.1 server built from scratch.

Everything talks to a stream with read(), write(), drain() and close(), the
same shape as asyncio's StreamReader and StreamWriter, so this code would run
on real sockets too. Here the streams come from a simulated network with a
simulated clock: a test with a thousand clients runs in a blink and gives the
same numbers every time.
"""
import asyncio
import bisect
import gzip
import json
import math
import re
from collections import OrderedDict, deque


# ======================================================================
# Part 1. Simulated time (given)
# ======================================================================

class SimLoop(asyncio.BaseEventLoop):
    """An asyncio event loop whose clock jumps straight to the next timer.

    A normal loop sleeps until the next timer is due. This one moves its
    clock forward instead, so asyncio.sleep(10) takes no real time, and
    every run of the same program sees exactly the same times.
    """

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self._now = 0.0
        self._selector = self      # the base loop asks its selector to wait

    def time(self):
        return self._now

    def select(self, timeout):
        # The loop has nothing ready and asks to wait up to `timeout`.
        if timeout is None:
            raise RuntimeError("deadlock: every task is waiting, and no timer is set")
        self._now += timeout
        return []

    def _process_events(self, events):
        pass

    def _write_to_self(self):
        pass


def run_sim(main):
    """Like asyncio.run(main), on a simulated clock that starts at 0."""
    loop = SimLoop()
    # In the browser, this code already runs inside a task on the page's own
    # event loop. Step out of that loop and that task while ours runs.
    outer = asyncio._get_running_loop()
    outer_task = asyncio.current_task(outer) if outer is not None else None
    if outer_task is not None:
        asyncio.tasks._leave_task(outer, outer_task)
    asyncio._set_running_loop(None)
    try:
        task = loop.create_task(main)
        try:
            return loop.run_until_complete(task)
        finally:
            rest = [t for t in asyncio.all_tasks(loop) if not t.done()]
            for t in rest:
                t.cancel()
            if rest:
                loop.run_until_complete(asyncio.gather(*rest, return_exceptions=True))
            loop.close()
    finally:
        asyncio._set_running_loop(outer)
        if outer_task is not None:
            asyncio.tasks._enter_task(outer, outer_task)


def now():
    """The simulated time, in seconds since run_sim started."""
    return asyncio.get_running_loop().time()


# ======================================================================
# Part 2. The simulated network
# ======================================================================

class Network:
    """An in-memory network of stream connections that behaves like TCP.

    latency: seconds that data takes to reach the other end (one way).
    chunk:   the most bytes one read() returns, so a test can make a
             request arrive one byte at a time.
    """

    def __init__(self, latency=0.0, chunk=65536):
        raise NotImplementedError("milestone 1: Network.__init__")

    def listen(self, addr):
        raise NotImplementedError("milestone 1: Network.listen")

    async def connect(self, addr, host="client"):
        """Open a connection to addr. Like TCP's handshake, it takes one round trip."""
        raise NotImplementedError("milestone 1: Network.connect")


class _Waitable:
    """One task at a time can wait here until something changes."""

    _waiter = None

    async def _wait(self):
        raise NotImplementedError("milestone 1: _Waitable._wait")

    def _wake(self):
        raise NotImplementedError("milestone 1: _Waitable._wake")


class Listener(_Waitable):
    """A socket that listens at one address and hands out new connections."""

    def __init__(self, net, addr):
        raise NotImplementedError("milestone 1: Listener.__init__")

    def _arrive(self, stream):
        raise NotImplementedError("milestone 1: Listener._arrive")

    async def accept(self):
        raise NotImplementedError("milestone 1: Listener.accept")

    def close(self):
        raise NotImplementedError("milestone 1: Listener.close")


class Stream(_Waitable):
    """One end of a connection. read() returns what the other end wrote, in order."""

    def __init__(self, net, local, remote):
        raise NotImplementedError("milestone 1: Stream.__init__")

    def write(self, data):
        raise NotImplementedError("milestone 1: Stream.write")

    async def drain(self):
        """Wait until the send buffer has room. It always has room here."""
        raise NotImplementedError("milestone 1: Stream.drain")

    def write_eof(self):
        """Send EOF but keep reading: a half-close, like shutdown(SHUT_WR)."""
        raise NotImplementedError("milestone 1: Stream.write_eof")

    async def read(self, n=65536):
        raise NotImplementedError("milestone 1: Stream.read")

    def close(self):
        raise NotImplementedError("milestone 1: Stream.close")

    def _travel(self, item):
        # Called on the receiving end. Items land in the order they were
        # sent: each timer lands the oldest item still in flight.
        raise NotImplementedError("milestone 1: Stream._travel")

    def _land(self):
        raise NotImplementedError("milestone 1: Stream._land")


# ======================================================================
# Test tools (given: the checks use these; keep them as they are)
# ======================================================================

async def together(*coros):
    """Run coroutines at the same time, and return their results in order."""
    return list(await asyncio.gather(*coros))


async def sequence(*actions):
    """Run actions one after another, and return their results.

    Each action is called with the list of results so far; if it returns
    something awaitable, that is awaited. An exception becomes its name."""
    results = []
    for action in actions:
        try:
            value = action(results)
            if hasattr(value, "__await__"):
                value = await value
        except Exception as error:
            value = type(error).__name__
        results.append(value)
    return results


async def timed(awaitable):
    """(what awaitable gave, or the name of its exception; the seconds it took)."""
    start = now()
    try:
        value = await awaitable
    except Exception as error:
        value = type(error).__name__
    return value, round(now() - start, 6)


async def script(net, addr, steps):
    """A scripted client. Steps: ("send", data), ("wait", seconds), ("eof",).

    It reads everything the other side sends while it works through the
    steps, and returns (every byte received, the time the other side closed)."""
    stream = await net.connect(addr)
    received = bytearray()

    async def read_all():
        while True:
            data = await stream.read()
            if not data:
                return now()
            received.extend(data)

    reading = asyncio.create_task(read_all())
    for step in steps:
        if step[0] == "send":
            stream.write(step[1])
        elif step[0] == "wait":
            await asyncio.sleep(step[1])
        elif step[0] == "eof":
            stream.write_eof()
        else:
            raise ValueError(f"unknown step {step!r}")
    closed_at = await reading
    stream.close()
    return bytes(received), closed_at


async def recorder(listener, size=65536):
    """Accept one connection and read it to the end: [(time, piece), ...]."""
    stream = await listener.accept()
    pieces = []
    while True:
        data = await stream.read(size)
        if not data:
            stream.close()
            return pieces
        pieces.append((round(now(), 6), data))


async def echo(listener):
    """Accept one connection, send back everything it sends, and close at its EOF."""
    stream = await listener.accept()
    while True:
        data = await stream.read()
        if not data:
            stream.close()
            return
        stream.write(data)
--- solution
"""ORBIT ground station: an HTTP/1.1 server built from scratch.

Everything talks to a stream with read(), write(), drain() and close(), the
same shape as asyncio's StreamReader and StreamWriter, so this code would run
on real sockets too. Here the streams come from a simulated network with a
simulated clock: a test with a thousand clients runs in a blink and gives the
same numbers every time.
"""
import asyncio
import bisect
import gzip
import json
import math
import re
from collections import OrderedDict, deque


# ======================================================================
# Part 1. Simulated time (given)
# ======================================================================

class SimLoop(asyncio.BaseEventLoop):
    """An asyncio event loop whose clock jumps straight to the next timer.

    A normal loop sleeps until the next timer is due. This one moves its
    clock forward instead, so asyncio.sleep(10) takes no real time, and
    every run of the same program sees exactly the same times.
    """

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self._now = 0.0
        self._selector = self      # the base loop asks its selector to wait

    def time(self):
        return self._now

    def select(self, timeout):
        # The loop has nothing ready and asks to wait up to `timeout`.
        if timeout is None:
            raise RuntimeError("deadlock: every task is waiting, and no timer is set")
        self._now += timeout
        return []

    def _process_events(self, events):
        pass

    def _write_to_self(self):
        pass


def run_sim(main):
    """Like asyncio.run(main), on a simulated clock that starts at 0."""
    loop = SimLoop()
    # In the browser, this code already runs inside a task on the page's own
    # event loop. Step out of that loop and that task while ours runs.
    outer = asyncio._get_running_loop()
    outer_task = asyncio.current_task(outer) if outer is not None else None
    if outer_task is not None:
        asyncio.tasks._leave_task(outer, outer_task)
    asyncio._set_running_loop(None)
    try:
        task = loop.create_task(main)
        try:
            return loop.run_until_complete(task)
        finally:
            rest = [t for t in asyncio.all_tasks(loop) if not t.done()]
            for t in rest:
                t.cancel()
            if rest:
                loop.run_until_complete(asyncio.gather(*rest, return_exceptions=True))
            loop.close()
    finally:
        asyncio._set_running_loop(outer)
        if outer_task is not None:
            asyncio.tasks._enter_task(outer, outer_task)


def now():
    """The simulated time, in seconds since run_sim started."""
    return asyncio.get_running_loop().time()


# ======================================================================
# Part 2. The simulated network
# ======================================================================

class Network:
    """An in-memory network of stream connections that behaves like TCP.

    latency: seconds that data takes to reach the other end (one way).
    chunk:   the most bytes one read() returns, so a test can make a
             request arrive one byte at a time.
    """

    def __init__(self, latency=0.0, chunk=65536):
        if latency < 0 or chunk < 1:
            raise ValueError("latency must be at least 0 and chunk at least 1")
        self.latency = latency
        self.chunk = chunk
        self.listeners = {}
        self._next_port = 50000

    def listen(self, addr):
        addr = tuple(addr)
        if addr in self.listeners:
            raise OSError(f"address already in use: {addr}")
        listener = Listener(self, addr)
        self.listeners[addr] = listener
        return listener

    async def connect(self, addr, host="client"):
        """Open a connection to addr. Like TCP's handshake, it takes one round trip."""
        addr = tuple(addr)
        await asyncio.sleep(self.latency)              # the SYN travels there
        listener = self.listeners.get(addr)
        if listener is None:
            await asyncio.sleep(self.latency)          # the refusal travels back
            raise ConnectionRefusedError(f"nobody is listening on {addr}")
        local = (host, self._next_port)
        self._next_port += 1
        client = Stream(self, local, addr)
        server = Stream(self, addr, local)
        client.peer, server.peer = server, client
        listener._arrive(server)
        await asyncio.sleep(self.latency)              # the SYN-ACK travels back
        return client


class _Waitable:
    """One task at a time can wait here until something changes."""

    _waiter = None

    async def _wait(self):
        if self._waiter is not None:
            raise RuntimeError("another task is already waiting on this")
        self._waiter = asyncio.get_running_loop().create_future()
        try:
            await self._waiter
        finally:
            self._waiter = None

    def _wake(self):
        if self._waiter is not None and not self._waiter.done():
            self._waiter.set_result(None)


class Listener(_Waitable):
    """A socket that listens at one address and hands out new connections."""

    def __init__(self, net, addr):
        self.net = net
        self.addr = addr
        self.closed = False
        self._pending = deque()      # connected, not yet accepted

    def _arrive(self, stream):
        self._pending.append(stream)
        self._wake()

    async def accept(self):
        while not self._pending:
            if self.closed:
                raise OSError("the listener is closed")
            await self._wait()
        return self._pending.popleft()

    def close(self):
        if self.closed:
            return
        self.closed = True
        if self.net.listeners.get(self.addr) is self:
            del self.net.listeners[self.addr]
        while self._pending:                 # never accepted: those clients see EOF
            self._pending.popleft().close()
        self._wake()


class Stream(_Waitable):
    """One end of a connection. read() returns what the other end wrote, in order."""

    def __init__(self, net, local, remote):
        self.net = net
        self.local = local
        self.remote = remote
        self.peer = None
        self.closed = False
        self._buffer = bytearray()   # arrived, not read yet
        self._in_flight = deque()    # sent to us, still travelling (None is EOF)
        self._eof = False            # the other end will send nothing more
        self._sending = True

    def write(self, data):
        if self.closed or not self._sending:
            raise OSError("this stream can no longer send")
        if data:
            self.peer._travel(bytes(data))

    async def drain(self):
        """Wait until the send buffer has room. It always has room here."""
        if self.closed:
            raise OSError("this stream is closed")

    def write_eof(self):
        """Send EOF but keep reading: a half-close, like shutdown(SHUT_WR)."""
        if self._sending:
            self._sending = False
            self.peer._travel(None)

    async def read(self, n=65536):
        if n < 1:
            raise ValueError("read at least one byte")
        while not self._buffer and not self._eof:
            if self.closed:
                raise OSError("this stream is closed")
            await self._wait()
        if self.closed:
            raise OSError("this stream is closed")
        size = min(n, self.net.chunk, len(self._buffer))
        data = bytes(self._buffer[:size])
        del self._buffer[:size]
        return data

    def close(self):
        if self.closed:
            return
        self.write_eof()
        self.closed = True
        self._buffer.clear()
        self._wake()                 # a task waiting in read() gets OSError

    def _travel(self, item):
        # Called on the receiving end. Items land in the order they were
        # sent: each timer lands the oldest item still in flight.
        self._in_flight.append(item)
        asyncio.get_running_loop().call_later(self.net.latency, self._land)

    def _land(self):
        item = self._in_flight.popleft()
        if self.closed:
            return                   # nobody will read it: dropped
        if item is None:
            self._eof = True
        else:
            self._buffer += item
        self._wake()


# ======================================================================
# Test tools (given: the checks use these; keep them as they are)
# ======================================================================

async def together(*coros):
    """Run coroutines at the same time, and return their results in order."""
    return list(await asyncio.gather(*coros))


async def sequence(*actions):
    """Run actions one after another, and return their results.

    Each action is called with the list of results so far; if it returns
    something awaitable, that is awaited. An exception becomes its name."""
    results = []
    for action in actions:
        try:
            value = action(results)
            if hasattr(value, "__await__"):
                value = await value
        except Exception as error:
            value = type(error).__name__
        results.append(value)
    return results


async def timed(awaitable):
    """(what awaitable gave, or the name of its exception; the seconds it took)."""
    start = now()
    try:
        value = await awaitable
    except Exception as error:
        value = type(error).__name__
    return value, round(now() - start, 6)


async def script(net, addr, steps):
    """A scripted client. Steps: ("send", data), ("wait", seconds), ("eof",).

    It reads everything the other side sends while it works through the
    steps, and returns (every byte received, the time the other side closed)."""
    stream = await net.connect(addr)
    received = bytearray()

    async def read_all():
        while True:
            data = await stream.read()
            if not data:
                return now()
            received.extend(data)

    reading = asyncio.create_task(read_all())
    for step in steps:
        if step[0] == "send":
            stream.write(step[1])
        elif step[0] == "wait":
            await asyncio.sleep(step[1])
        elif step[0] == "eof":
            stream.write_eof()
        else:
            raise ValueError(f"unknown step {step!r}")
    closed_at = await reading
    stream.close()
    return bytes(received), closed_at


async def recorder(listener, size=65536):
    """Accept one connection and read it to the end: [(time, piece), ...]."""
    stream = await listener.accept()
    pieces = []
    while True:
        data = await stream.read(size)
        if not data:
            stream.close()
            return pieces
        pieces.append((round(now(), 6), data))


async def echo(listener):
    """Accept one connection, send back everything it sends, and close at its EOF."""
    stream = await listener.accept()
    while True:
        data = await stream.read()
        if not data:
            stream.close()
            return
        stream.write(data)
--- hint
Start with `_Waitable`, then `Stream`: most of the network is in it. `_travel` and `_land` are the heart: `_travel` only queues the item and sets a timer, and `_land` always takes `self._in_flight.popleft()`, never data passed to it.
--- hint
`read` loops `while not self._buffer and not self._eof:`, raising `OSError` inside the loop if `self.closed`, and otherwise `await self._wait()`. After the loop, slice `self._buffer[:size]` into `bytes`, then `del self._buffer[:size]`.
--- hint
`connect` is three steps with two or three sleeps: sleep, look up the listener (refuse after a second sleep if there is none), make and link the two streams, `listener._arrive(server_end)`, sleep, return the client's end. `Listener.accept` is a loop like `read`'s, around `self._pending`.

+++ practice | A delay line for telemetry frames
--- task
A radio link delays every telemetry frame by the same time. Write a class `DelayLine(delay)` over the simulated clock in the starter:

- `put(frame)` sends a frame (any object) and returns at once. The frame becomes available `delay` seconds later.
- `async get()` returns the oldest frame that has become available, waiting until one has if there is none yet.

Frames must come out in the order they were put, even when several are put at the same moment. Use `asyncio.get_running_loop().call_later` for the delay, a `deque` of frames in flight, and a future to wake a waiting `get`. Only one task calls `get` at a time.

The starter's `arrivals(line, send_times)` (given) puts frame `k` at time `send_times[k]` and returns `(frame, time got)` for each frame. For example, `run_sim(arrivals(DelayLine(0.25), [0.0, 0.1]))` gives `[(0, 0.25), (1, 0.35)]`.
--- starter
import asyncio


class SimLoop(asyncio.BaseEventLoop):
    """An asyncio event loop on simulated time (given)."""

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self._now = 0.0
        self._selector = self

    def time(self):
        return self._now

    def select(self, timeout):
        if timeout is None:
            raise RuntimeError("deadlock: every task is waiting, and no timer is set")
        self._now += timeout
        return []

    def _process_events(self, events):
        pass

    def _write_to_self(self):
        pass


def run_sim(main):
    """Like asyncio.run(main), on simulated time (given)."""
    loop = SimLoop()
    # In the browser, this code already runs inside a task on the page's own
    # event loop. Step out of that loop and that task while ours runs.
    outer = asyncio._get_running_loop()
    outer_task = asyncio.current_task(outer) if outer is not None else None
    if outer_task is not None:
        asyncio.tasks._leave_task(outer, outer_task)
    asyncio._set_running_loop(None)
    try:
        task = loop.create_task(main)
        try:
            return loop.run_until_complete(task)
        finally:
            rest = [t for t in asyncio.all_tasks(loop) if not t.done()]
            for t in rest:
                t.cancel()
            if rest:
                loop.run_until_complete(asyncio.gather(*rest, return_exceptions=True))
            loop.close()
    finally:
        asyncio._set_running_loop(outer)
        if outer_task is not None:
            asyncio.tasks._enter_task(outer, outer_task)


def now():
    """The simulated time in seconds (given)."""
    return asyncio.get_running_loop().time()
from collections import deque


class DelayLine:
    def __init__(self, delay):
        self.delay = delay

    def put(self, frame):
        raise NotImplementedError

    async def sender():
        for k, t in enumerate(send_times):
            await asyncio.sleep(t - now())
            line.put(k)

    task = asyncio.get_running_loop().create_task(sender())
    got = []
    for _ in send_times:
        frame = await line.get()
        got.append((frame, round(now(), 6)))
    await task
    return got

    def _process_events(self, events):
        pass

    def _write_to_self(self):
        pass

from collections import deque


class DelayLine:
    def __init__(self, delay):
        self.delay = delay
        self.in_flight = deque()    # put, not arrived yet
        self.arrived = deque()      # arrived, not got yet
        self.waiter = None

    def put(self, frame):
        self.in_flight.append(frame)
        asyncio.get_running_loop().call_later(self.delay, self._arrive)

    def _arrive(self):
        # Timers due together fire in any order: move the oldest frame, not "this" one.
        self.arrived.append(self.in_flight.popleft())
        if self.waiter is not None and not self.waiter.done():
            self.waiter.set_result(None)

    async def get(self):
        while not self.arrived:
            self.waiter = asyncio.get_running_loop().create_future()
            try:
                await self.waiter
            finally:
                self.waiter = None
        return self.arrived.popleft()


async def arrivals(line, send_times):
    """Put frame k at send_times[k]; return (frame, time it was got) for each (given)."""
    async def sender():
        for k, t in enumerate(send_times):
            await asyncio.sleep(t - now())
            line.put(k)

    task = asyncio.get_running_loop().create_task(sender())
    got = []
    for _ in send_times:
        frame = await line.get()
        got.append((frame, round(now(), 6)))
    await task
    return got
--- hint
Keep two deques: frames in flight and frames that have arrived. `put` appends to the first and sets a timer; the timer's callback moves the oldest frame in flight to the second.
--- hint
`get` loops while nothing has arrived: make a future with `asyncio.get_running_loop().create_future()`, keep it in an attribute, and await it. The timer's callback sets its result, if it is not done yet.
--- check case | Frames sent at different times arrive delay seconds after each
run_sim(arrivals(DelayLine(0.25), [0.0, 0.1, 1.0]))
=> [(0, 0.25), (1, 0.35), (2, 1.25)]
--- check test | Twenty frames sent in the same instant keep their order
run_sim(arrivals(DelayLine(0.1), [0.0] * 20)) == [(k, 0.1) for k in range(20)]
?? Timers due at the same moment fire in any order. Move the oldest frame in flight, not one passed to the callback.
--- check case | A zero delay still delivers, in order
run_sim(arrivals(DelayLine(0), [0.0, 0.0, 0.5]))
=> [(0, 0.0), (1, 0.0), (2, 0.5)]
--- check case | Frames can be any object
run_sim((lambda line: arrivals(line, [0.0, 0.0]))(DelayLine(1)))
=> [(0, 1.0), (1, 1.0)]

+++ practice | When does each message arrive?
--- task
Real links also have a **bandwidth**: they put `bandwidth` bytes a second on the wire, one message at a time. A message sent at time `t` starts going out at `t`, or when the message before it has finished going out, whichever is later. It takes `size / bandwidth` seconds to go out, and arrives `latency` seconds after it has finished.

Write `arrival_times(sends, latency, bandwidth)`. `sends` is a list of `(time, size)` pairs in the order they were sent, with times that never go down. Return the arrival time of each message, in the same order, each rounded to 6 decimal places with `round(x, 6)`. No messages gives `[]`.

For example, `arrival_times([(0, 1000), (0, 1000)], 0.1, 10000)` gives `[0.2, 0.3]`: the first goes out from 0 to 0.1 and arrives at 0.2; the second waits, goes out from 0.1 to 0.2, and arrives at 0.3.
--- starter
def arrival_times(sends, latency, bandwidth):
    return [round(t + latency, 6) for t, size in sends]
--- solution
def arrival_times(sends, latency, bandwidth):
    arrivals = []
    link_free = 0.0                     # when the link finishes its current message
    for sent, size in sends:
        start = max(sent, link_free)
        link_free = start + size / bandwidth
        arrivals.append(round(link_free + latency, 6))
    return arrivals
--- hint
Keep one number as you go: the time the link becomes free. A message starts at the later of its send time and that time.
--- hint
After a message starts, the link is free again `size / bandwidth` seconds later, and the message arrives `latency` after that.
--- check case | The example from the task: the second message queues
arrival_times([(0, 1000), (0, 1000)], 0.1, 10000)
=> [0.2, 0.3]
--- check case | Messages far apart never queue
arrival_times([(0, 500), (5, 500)], 0.02, 1000)
=> [0.52, 5.52]
--- check case | A big message delays the small one behind it
arrival_times([(0, 8000), (0.1, 10)], 0.05, 10000)
=> [0.85, 0.851]
--- check case | No messages
arrival_times([], 0.1, 1000)
=> []
--- check case | A message of size 0 still pays the latency
arrival_times([(1, 0)], 0.25, 1000)
=> [1.25]

+++ practice | A mailbox that gives up
--- task
A ground station waits for replies from a probe, but not forever. Write a class `Mailbox` over the simulated clock:

- `deliver(message)` adds a message.
- `async receive(timeout)` returns the oldest message not yet received, waiting for one if needed. If none comes within `timeout` seconds, it returns `None`.

Use a deque and a future, as the network does, and `asyncio.wait_for` for the timeout; it raises `asyncio.TimeoutError` when the time runs out. A message delivered after a receive gave up must still be there for the next receive.

The starter's `conversation(box, deliveries, timeouts)` (given) delivers each `(time, message)` in `deliveries` at its time, and runs the receives one after another with the given timeouts, returning `(result, time)` for each.
--- starter

        pass

        pass

                t.cancel()
            if rest:

from collections import deque


class Mailbox:
    def __init__(self):
        self.messages = deque()

    def deliver(self, message):
        self.messages.append(message)

    async def receive(self, timeout):
        return self.messages.popleft() if self.messages else None


async def conversation(box, deliveries, timeouts):
    """Deliver each (time, message) at its time; receive once per timeout, in turn (given)."""
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    for t, message in deliveries:
        loop.call_later(t, box.deliver, message)
    results = []
    for timeout in timeouts:
        got = await box.receive(timeout)
        results.append((got, round(now(), 6)))
    return results

import asyncio


class SimLoop(asyncio.BaseEventLoop):
    """An asyncio event loop on simulated time (given)."""

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self._now = 0.0
        self._selector = self

    def time(self):
        return self._now

    def select(self, timeout):
        if timeout is None:
            raise RuntimeError("deadlock: every task is waiting, and no timer is set")
        self._now += timeout
        return []

    def _process_events(self, events):
        pass

    def _write_to_self(self):
        pass


def run_sim(main):
    """Like asyncio.run(main), on simulated time (given)."""
    loop = SimLoop()
    # In the browser, this code already runs inside a task on the page's own
    # event loop. Step out of that loop and that task while ours runs.
    outer = asyncio._get_running_loop()

    if outer_task is not None:
        asyncio.tasks._leave_task(outer, outer_task)
    asyncio._set_running_loop(None)
    try:
        task = loop.create_task(main)
        try:
            return loop.run_until_complete(task)
        finally:
            rest = [t for t in asyncio.all_tasks(loop) if not t.done()]
            for t in rest:
                t.cancel()
            if rest:
                loop.run_until_complete(asyncio.gather(*rest, return_exceptions=True))
            loop.close()
    finally:
        asyncio._set_running_loop(outer)
        if outer_task is not None:
            asyncio.tasks._enter_task(outer, outer_task)


def now():
    """The simulated time in seconds (given)."""
    return asyncio.get_running_loop().time()
from collections import deque


class Mailbox:
    def __init__(self):
        self.messages = deque()
        self.waiter = None

    def deliver(self, message):
        self.messages.append(message)
        if self.waiter is not None and not self.waiter.done():
            self.waiter.set_result(None)

    async def _wait_for_message(self):
        while not self.messages:
            self.waiter = asyncio.get_running_loop().create_future()
            try:
                await self.waiter
            finally:
                self.waiter = None
        return self.messages.popleft()

    async def receive(self, timeout):
        try:
            return await asyncio.wait_for(self._wait_for_message(), timeout)
        except asyncio.TimeoutError:
            return None


async def conversation(box, deliveries, timeouts):
    """Deliver each (time, message) at its time; receive once per timeout, in turn (given)."""
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    for t, message in deliveries:
        loop.call_later(t, box.deliver, message)
    results = []
    for timeout in timeouts:
        got = await box.receive(timeout)
        results.append((got, round(now(), 6)))
    return results
--- hint
Write a helper coroutine that waits, with a future, until a message is there and then pops it. `deliver` wakes the waiting future.
--- hint
`receive` wraps that helper in `asyncio.wait_for(helper(), timeout)` and turns `asyncio.TimeoutError` into `None`. When `wait_for` gives up, it cancels the helper while it waits, so the helper must not have taken a message yet.
--- check case | A message that comes in time is returned when it comes
run_sim(conversation(Mailbox(), [(0.4, "ack")], [1.0]))
=> [("ack", 0.4)]
--- check case | Nothing in time: None, after exactly the timeout
run_sim(conversation(Mailbox(), [], [2.5]))
=> [(None, 2.5)]
--- check case | A late message waits for the next receive
run_sim(conversation(Mailbox(), [(3, "late")], [1, 5]))
=> [(None, 1.0), ("late", 3.0)]
--- check case | Messages already there come back at once, oldest first
run_sim(conversation(Mailbox(), [(0, "a"), (0, "b")], [1, 1, 1]))
=> [("a", 0.0), ("b", 0.0), (None, 1.0)]

+++ practice | Reading exactly n bytes
--- task
A stream's `read(n)` returns **up to** `n` bytes, so a program that needs exactly n bytes must loop. Write `async read_exactly(stream, n)`:

- It returns exactly `n` bytes, calling `await stream.read(n - got)` as often as it takes.
- `n == 0` returns `b""` without reading.
- A negative `n` raises `ValueError`.
- If the stream reaches EOF (a read returns `b""`) first, raise `EOFError`.

The starter's `PieceStream(data, chunk)` (given) is a stream whose reads return at most `chunk` bytes of `data`, then `b""` forever. For example, `run_sim(read_exactly(PieceStream(b"orbit", 2), 3))` gives `b"orb"`.
--- starter

class PieceStream:
    """A stream over fixed data, at most `chunk` bytes per read (given)."""

    def __init__(self, data, chunk):
        self.data = data
        self.chunk = chunk
        self.reads = 0

    async def read(self, n):
        self.reads += 1
        await asyncio.sleep(0.001)
        piece = self.data[:min(n, self.chunk)]
        self.data = self.data[len(piece):]
        return piece


async def read_exactly(stream, n):
    return await stream.read(n)

class PieceStream:
    """A stream over fixed data, at most `chunk` bytes per read (given)."""

    def __init__(self, data, chunk):
        self.data = data
        self.chunk = chunk
        self.reads = 0

    async def read(self, n):
        self.reads += 1
        await asyncio.sleep(0.001)
        piece = self.data[:min(n, self.chunk)]
        self.data = self.data[len(piece):]
        return piece


async def read_exactly(stream, n):
    if n < 0:
        raise ValueError("n must not be negative")
    parts = []
    got = 0
    while got < n:
        piece = await stream.read(n - got)
        if not piece:
            raise EOFError(f"the stream ended after {got} of {n} bytes")
        parts.append(piece)
        got += len(piece)
    return b"".join(parts)
--- hint
Loop while you have fewer than `n` bytes, asking each time for only the bytes still missing, so you never read into the next message.
--- hint
Collect the pieces in a list and join them once at the end. A piece of `b""` means EOF: raise `EOFError` then.
--- check case | Pieces of 2 bytes, 3 wanted
run_sim(read_exactly(PieceStream(b"orbit", 2), 3))
=> b"orb"
--- check case | One byte at a time takes n reads, and leaves the rest unread
(lambda s: (run_sim(read_exactly(s, 4)), s.reads, s.data))(PieceStream(b"telemetry", 1))
=> (b"tele", 4, b"metry")
--- check case | n = 0 reads nothing
(lambda s: (run_sim(read_exactly(s, 0)), s.reads))(PieceStream(b"abc", 5))
=> (b"", 0)
--- check test | EOF before n bytes raises EOFError
raises(EOFError, lambda: run_sim(read_exactly(PieceStream(b"ab", 5), 3)))
--- check test | A negative n raises ValueError
raises(ValueError, lambda: run_sim(read_exactly(PieceStream(b"ab", 5), -1)))
--- check case | Exactly all the data
run_sim(read_exactly(PieceStream(b"xyz", 10), 3))
=> b"xyz"

+++ practice | Debug: the link that scrambles bytes
--- task
The starter's `Link` carries bytes from `send` to `receive` after a delay, like one direction of the network you built. It passes a test with one message, but when several messages are sent in the same instant, they come out in a scrambled order: `b"GET / HTTP/1.1"` sent in pieces can arrive as `b" /GETHTTP/1.1 "`.

Find the bug and fix it, so that bytes always arrive in the order they were sent, each piece `delay` seconds after it was sent. Keep the method names.

from collections import deque


class Link:
    def __init__(self, delay):
        self.delay = delay
        self.buffer = bytearray()
        self.waiter = None

    def send(self, data):
        asyncio.get_running_loop().call_later(self.delay, self._land, data)

    def _land(self, data):
        self.buffer += data
        if self.waiter is not None and not self.waiter.done():
            self.waiter.set_result(None)

    async def receive(self):
        while not self.buffer:
            self.waiter = asyncio.get_running_loop().create_future()
            try:
                await self.waiter
            finally:
                self.waiter = None
        data = bytes(self.buffer)
        self.buffer.clear()
        return data

    for piece in pieces:
        link.send(piece)
    got = b""
    while len(got) < total:
        got += await link.receive()
    return got, now()

from collections import deque


class Link:
    def __init__(self, delay):
        self.delay = delay
        self.buffer = bytearray()
        self.in_flight = deque()
        self.waiter = None

    def send(self, data):
        self.in_flight.append(bytes(data))
        asyncio.get_running_loop().call_later(self.delay, self._land)

    def _land(self):
        # Timers due at the same moment fire in any order, so land the oldest piece.
        self.buffer += self.in_flight.popleft()
        if self.waiter is not None and not self.waiter.done():
            self.waiter.set_result(None)

    async def receive(self):
        while not self.buffer:
            self.waiter = asyncio.get_running_loop().create_future()
            try:
                await self.waiter
            finally:
                self.waiter = None
        data = bytes(self.buffer)
        self.buffer.clear()
        return data


async def send_all(link, pieces, total):
    """Send every piece at once, then receive until `total` bytes have come (given)."""
    for piece in pieces:
        link.send(piece)
    got = b""
    while len(got) < total:
        got += await link.receive()
    return got, now()
--- hint
Each timer carries its own piece of data. What order do timers that are due at exactly the same moment fire in?
--- hint
Keep the pieces in a `deque` when they are sent, and let each timer land the oldest piece still in flight, whatever order the timers fire in.
--- check case | Pieces sent together arrive in order
run_sim(send_all(Link(0.1), [b"GET", b" ", b"/", b" ", b"HTTP/1.1"], 14))
=> (b"GET / HTTP/1.1", 0.1)
--- check test | Fifty pieces in one instant arrive in order
run_sim(send_all(Link(0.05), [b"%d;" % i for i in range(50)], len(b"".join(b"%d;" % i for i in range(50)))))[0] == b"".join(b"%d;" % i for i in range(50))
--- check case | One piece arrives after the delay
run_sim(send_all(Link(0.3), [b"ping"], 4))
=> (b"ping", 0.3)

+++ practice | A relay between two connections
--- task
A relay (a TCP proxy) sits between a client and a server and copies bytes both ways. The starter gives `pair()`, which makes the two ends of an in-memory connection with no delay. Each end has `write(data)`, `write_eof()` and `async read()`, which returns the next piece, or `b""` once EOF has arrived (and every time after).

Write `async relay(client, server)`. `client` is the relay's end of the connection from the client, and `server` its end of the connection to the server. Copy everything from `client` to `server` and everything from `server` to `client`, **both at the same time**. When one direction reaches EOF, pass it on with `write_eof()` on the other end, but keep copying the other direction. Once both directions have ended, return `(bytes copied to the server, bytes copied to the client)`.

The starter's `run_relay(request, respond)` (given) runs a client and a server with your relay between them. The client sends `request`, one line, and waits for a one-line answer before it sends EOF. The server answers `respond(the line it got)` as soon as it has the line, then waits for EOF and sends its own. It returns the answer the client got and your relay's result.
--- starter

def now():
    """The simulated time in seconds (given)."""
    return asyncio.get_running_loop().time()


class End:
    """One end of an in-memory connection (given)."""

    def __init__(self):
        self.inbox = asyncio.Queue()
        self.peer = None
        self.at_eof = False

    def write(self, data):
        if data:
            self.peer.inbox.put_nowait(bytes(data))

    def write_eof(self):
        self.peer.inbox.put_nowait(b"")

    async def read(self):
        if self.at_eof:
            return b""
        data = await self.inbox.get()
        self.at_eof = data == b""
        return data


def pair():
    a, b = End(), End()
    a.peer, b.peer = b, a
    return a, b


async def relay(client, server):
    return 0, 0


async def run_relay(request, respond):
    """A client, a server and your relay between them (given)."""
    client_side, relay_client = pair()
    relay_server, server_side = pair()

    async def read_line(end):
        got = b""
        while not got.endswith(b"\n"):
            piece = await end.read()
            if not piece:
                break
            got += piece
        return got

    async def client():
        for i in range(0, len(request), 3):
            client_side.write(request[i:i + 3])
            await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
        answer = await read_line(client_side)
        client_side.write_eof()
        while await client_side.read():
            pass
        return answer

    async def server():
        line = await read_line(server_side)
        server_side.write(respond(line))
        while await server_side.read():
            pass
        server_side.write_eof()

    results = await asyncio.gather(client(), server(), relay(relay_client, relay_server))
    return results[0], results[2]


async def timed(awaitable):
    """(what awaitable gave, the simulated seconds it took) (given)."""
    start = now()
    value = await awaitable
    return value, round(now() - start, 6)

class End:
    """One end of an in-memory connection (given)."""

    def __init__(self):
        self.inbox = asyncio.Queue()
        self.peer = None
        self.at_eof = False

    def write(self, data):
        if data:
            self.peer.inbox.put_nowait(bytes(data))

    def write_eof(self):
        self.peer.inbox.put_nowait(b"")

    async def read(self):
        if self.at_eof:
            return b""
        data = await self.inbox.get()
        self.at_eof = data == b""
        return data


def pair():
    a, b = End(), End()
    a.peer, b.peer = b, a
    return a, b


async def copy(source, target):
    """Copy until EOF, pass the EOF on, and return how many bytes went across."""
    total = 0
    while True:
        data = await source.read()
        if not data:
            target.write_eof()
            return total
        target.write(data)
        total += len(data)


async def relay(client, server):
    up, down = await asyncio.gather(copy(client, server), copy(server, client))
    return up, down


async def run_relay(request, respond):
    """A client, a server and your relay between them (given)."""
    client_side, relay_client = pair()
    relay_server, server_side = pair()

    async def read_line(end):
        got = b""
        while not got.endswith(b"\n"):
            piece = await end.read()
            if not piece:
                break
            got += piece
        return got

    async def client():
        for i in range(0, len(request), 3):
            client_side.write(request[i:i + 3])
            await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
        answer = await read_line(client_side)
        client_side.write_eof()
        while await client_side.read():
            pass
        return answer

    async def server():
        line = await read_line(server_side)
        server_side.write(respond(line))
        while await server_side.read():
            pass
        server_side.write_eof()

    results = await asyncio.gather(client(), server(), relay(relay_client, relay_server))
    return results[0], results[2]


async def timed(awaitable):
    """(what awaitable gave, the simulated seconds it took) (given)."""
    start = now()
    value = await awaitable
    return value, round(now() - start, 6)

=== cap-http-02 | An incremental parser I: the request line and headers
--- teach
Last milestone you built a network that can deliver a request in pieces of any size, even one byte at a time. Now the server must turn those pieces into requests. This milestone builds the first half of the parser: the request line and the headers, with the limits and error codes a server on the open Internet needs. Bodies come next milestone.

### The job

A request's **head** is a request line, header lines, and an empty line, each ended by CR LF:

```text
GET /telemetry/latest?sensor=temp HTTP/1.1\r\n
Host: gs.orbit\r\n
Accept: application/json\r\n
\r\n
```

The parser receives bytes as they arrive and must hand the server one `Request` object per request, in order. For anything malformed it must say which **status code** the server should answer with, because a good server tells a client what it did wrong:

| problem | status |
|---|---|
| a malformed line: bad method, bad target, a space before a colon, a bare CR or LF | 400 Bad Request |
| an HTTP/1.1 request without exactly one Host header | 400 Bad Request |
| a request line longer than `max_line` bytes | 414 URI Too Long |
| header lines over `max_head` bytes in total, or more than `max_headers` of them | 431 Request Header Fields Too Large |
| a well-formed version that is not 1.0 or 1.1, such as `HTTP/2.0` | 505 HTTP Version Not Supported |

An error is raised as `HTTPError(status, message)`, an exception that carries the status to send.

### Design choice 1: incremental, not "wait for the whole head"

In the networks course, `parse_requests` waited until `\r\n\r\n` had arrived and then parsed the head in one go. That is simple, and it has two problems:

- **Limits come too late.** A client can send a megabyte of header without ever sending the empty line. A server that waits for `\r\n\r\n` before it looks at anything buffers all of it. An incremental parser checks every line against its limit while the line is still arriving, and refuses as soon as the limit is passed.
- **Bodies need state anyway.** Next milestone, a chunked body arrives as a sequence of pieces with sizes. The parser must remember where it is between one piece of network data and the next. That is a **state machine**: a small set of named states, and rules for moving between them.

So the parser keeps a **state**, `"start"` (waiting for a request line) or `"headers"`, and handles one complete line at a time. When a line has not fully arrived, it stops and waits for more bytes.

### Design choice 2: feed, then pull

There are three common shapes for a parser's interface:

1. **Callbacks**, as in Node.js's parser: "call my function when a header arrives". Fast, but the server's logic gets split across many small functions.
2. **`feed(data)` returns every request that is now complete.** Simple, but if the second request in a piece is broken, the exception loses the first, good request.
3. **`feed(data)` stores the bytes; `next_message()` returns the next complete request, or `None`.** It raises `HTTPError` only when it reaches the broken request.

This project uses the third, which is also how the Python library h11 works. The server answers requests one at a time, so it pulls one, answers it, pulls the next. A good request before a broken one is still answered, and requests the server has not reached yet simply wait in the buffer. Once `next_message` has raised, it raises the same error every time: the byte stream is out of step, and nothing after the error can be trusted.

### The data: a buffer and a scan position

The parser keeps received bytes in `self._buf`, a `bytearray`. To take a line, it searches for `b"\r\n"`:

```python
buf = bytearray(b"PUT /config HTTP/1.1\r\nHo")
end = buf.find(b"\r\n")
print(end, bytes(buf[:end]))      # 20 b'PUT /config HTTP/1.1'
del buf[:end + 2]
print(buf)                        # bytearray(b'Ho'): the next line has begun
```

When the next line has not all arrived, the search fails. Searching the whole buffer again after every new piece would cost O(n²) for a head of n bytes that arrives one byte at a time. So the parser remembers, in `self._scan`, where the next search may start: everything before it is known to hold no CR LF. It cannot be the very last byte, though: a CR at the end may be the first half of a CR LF whose LF has not arrived yet. So after a failed search, `_scan = len(buf) - 1`, and after taking a line, `_scan = 0`.

**Why it is linear.** Each byte is looked at by `find` at most twice: once when it is new, and once more if it was the last byte of a failed search. So the searching costs O(n) in total for n bytes, however they are cut up. Deleting from the front of a `bytearray` does not move the bytes behind, so taking lines is O(n) in total too.

### Taking a line, with its limit

One helper, `_take_line(limit, status)`, does the searching for every state. It returns the next line without its CR LF, or `None` if the line has not all arrived. It raises `HTTPError(status)` if the line is longer than `limit`, and it checks that even when the line is not complete yet. That is what stops the megabyte-of-header attack: the parser holds at most `limit` bytes of an unfinished line. It also raises 400 if the finished line holds a lone CR or LF.

The limit depends on the state: `max_line` (and status 414) for the request line, and for a header line, whatever is left of `max_head` (status 431) after the header lines so far.

### The grammar, one line at a time

**The request line** is exactly three parts, split by single spaces: `METHOD TARGET VERSION`.

- The method must be a **[[token|token]]**: one or more of the letters, digits and ``!#$%&'*+-.^_`|~``. So `GET` and `M-SEARCH` pass, while `G(T` and an empty method fail.
- The target must be ASCII with no spaces or control characters, and start with `/`. The one exception is `*`, only for `OPTIONS`. Proxies also accept a full URL there; this server is not a proxy, so it rejects them.
- The version must look like `HTTP/1.1`: `HTTP/`, a digit, a dot, a digit. A version of that shape other than 1.0 and 1.1 gets 505. Anything else gets 400.

**A header line** is `name: value`:

- The name is a token, and it ends right at the colon. A space before the colon is a 400: some servers ignore it and some treat the space as part of the name, and a request two servers read differently is how **[[request smuggling|smuggling]]** attacks begin.
- Split at the **first** colon only, with `partition`, since values such as `Host: gs:8080` hold colons of their own.
- Spaces and tabs around the value do not count. Control characters inside it are a 400.
- A line that starts with a space or tab is an old way of continuing the previous header, called obs-fold. It is a 400 too.

The bytes of a header value are turned into text with [[Latin-1|latin1]], which maps each byte to one character and can never fail.

**At the empty line** the head is complete. An HTTP/1.1 request must then have exactly one `Host` header.

### Headers: not a dict

A plain dict loses information HTTP needs: a name may appear twice (`Accept: a` and then `accept: b`), and names are compared without case. So `Headers` keeps a list of `(name, value)` pairs, in order, with the names exactly as sent:

- `get(name)` joins every value of that name with `", "`, which is how HTTP combines repeated headers, and returns a default if there is none;
- `get_all(name)` returns the values as a list; `name in headers`, `headers[name]` and `headers[name] = value` work as on a dict, and `remove(name)` removes them all;
- `tokens(name)` returns the lower-case, comma-separated tokens of a header as a set, which is what `Connection: keep-alive, Upgrade` needs.

Every lookup scans the list, O(h) for h headers. With at most 100 headers that is cheaper than keeping a second, lower-cased dict in step.

### The request, and the target

The parser builds a `Request(method, target, version, headers, body)`. It keeps the raw `target`, and splits it at the first `?` into:

- `path`, with its **[[percent-encoding|percent]]** undone: `/files/a%20b.txt` becomes `/files/a b.txt`;
- `query`, a dict: `sensor=temp&x=1+2` gives `{"sensor": "temp", "x": "1 2"}`. In a query, `+` also means a space; a name without `=` gets `""`; a repeated name keeps its last value.

`keep_alive()` says whether the client wants the connection kept open: HTTP/1.1 does unless `Connection` holds the token `close`; HTTP/1.0 does only if it holds `keep-alive`. `params` and `remote` start empty and are filled in later by the router and the server.

### One parser, two kinds of message

In milestone 4 the client will read responses with exactly the same framing. So the machinery lives in a base class, `MessageParser`, and a subclass fills in three **hooks**:

- `_parse_start(line)` reads the first line, and returns what it found;
- `_end_of_head()` runs at the empty line: checks, and choosing the next state;
- `_make_message()` builds the finished object.

`RequestParser` fills them in for requests. `next_message()` in the base class loops: it asks `_advance()` to take one step at a time, until the state is `"done"` or more bytes are needed. At `"done"` it builds the message, resets the per-message fields, and goes back to `"start"`. Blank lines before a request line are skipped, as the standard asks.

**The invariant that makes it correct:** *`_buf` holds exactly the bytes received and not yet used, and `_state` says what those bytes must be the start of.* Taking a line removes exactly one line from the front and moves to the state for what follows it, so the invariant holds after every step, however the bytes were cut. The random-cuts check tests exactly this.

`idle` is `True` when the parser is between messages and holds no byte of the next one. Milestone 11 will use it to tell an idle connection from one halfway through a request.

### How to test it

`parse_requests(data, piece=None, **limits)` feeds `data` to a new parser in pieces of `piece` bytes (all at once by default), pulls every complete request after each piece, and returns the list. The checks compare cutting into 1-byte pieces, random pieces and one piece: all must give the same requests. The test tool `error_status(data, ...)` returns the status of the `HTTPError` that `parse_requests` raises, or `None`.

**Watch out:**

- Checking a line's length only once the line is complete. A client that never sends CR LF then fills your memory.
- Resetting `_scan` to the end of the buffer instead of one byte before it. A CR LF split across two pieces is then never found.
- Splitting a header line with `split(":")` instead of `partition(":")`, which breaks on `Host: gs:8080`.
- Forgetting to reset the headers between requests on one connection, so the second request carries the first one's headers too.

::: context token Tokens: the safe characters
RFC 9110, the standard for HTTP's meaning, defines a token as one or more "tchar" characters: letters, digits, and fifteen symbols (``!#$%&'*+-.^_`|~``). Methods, header names and many header values are tokens. The list leaves out spaces, colons, quotes, brackets and slashes, which are the characters that separate things in HTTP syntax. Checking with a `frozenset` of the allowed byte values is O(1) per byte, so checking a name of k bytes is O(k).
:::

::: context smuggling When two servers disagree about one request
Most sites put a proxy, a load balancer or a CDN in front of their servers, and it sends many users' requests to a server over one kept-alive connection. If the proxy and the server parse a request differently, for example one ignores `Content-Length : 5` with its stray space and the other obeys it, they disagree about where the request ends. An attacker then hides a second request inside the first one's body, and the server runs it as if it came from the next user. The defence is strictness: reject anything ambiguous with 400.
:::

::: context latin1 Why Latin-1 for header bytes
HTTP headers are defined as bytes, and should be ASCII, but real clients sometimes send other bytes. Latin-1 (ISO-8859-1) maps every byte 0 to 255 to the character with the same number, so decoding never fails and encoding the text back gives exactly the original bytes. UTF-8 would fail on some byte sequences, and a parser must never crash on input. That is why Python's own `http.server` and many other servers decode headers as Latin-1.
:::

::: context percent Percent-encoding
A URL may only contain certain ASCII characters, so anything else is written as a percent sign and two hex digits per byte: a space is `%20`, and `é`, which is two bytes in UTF-8, is `%C3%A9`. Decoding turns each `%XX` back into its byte, and then decodes the bytes as UTF-8. A broken escape such as `%zz` is left as it is. A decoded path can contain `/` from `%2F`, and `..`, which is why milestone 9 will check paths again before it touches any file.
:::
